23: ## 325944: double intervals; two developed routes and the exact unpaid step
24: 
25: Source 1307.5094 defines a(S) as the maximum NUMBER of approving voters, and a(S)/n as approval ratio. The record calls a(S) a ratio, an internal transcription inconsistency. We investigate the intended source inequality, not manufacture credit from dividing an already normalized ratio by n. Approval sets consist of two disjoint closed intervals on one common line. Pairwise intersecting means intersections of whole approval sets, not every individual component pair.
26: 
27: Route A: endpoint accounting, including the source's strengthened boundary correction. Write a for maximum depth; each voter contributes intervals A_i,A'_i. Define L,R,B,C of a component I as the numbers of other components covering just its left endpoint, just its right endpoint, both endpoints, or lying in its interior. Each voter meets every other voter, so the sum over its two components of L+R+B+C is at least n-1. Summing gives n(n-1)≤Σ(L+R+B+C). A containing pair contributes once to B at the inner interval and once to C at the outer, hence ΣB=ΣC.
28: 
29: No point is in more than a intervals: a voter's own components are disjoint. Initial endpoint capacities are Σ(L+B)≤2n(a-1) and Σ(R+B)≤2n(a-1). Order the 2n left endpoints. The first a positions have capacities 0,1,...,a-1 instead of all a-1, saving a(a-1)/2; order right endpoints from the right for the same saving. Thus
30: n(n-1) ≤ 4n(a-1)-a(a-1) = (4n-a)(a-1).
31: Solving this quadratic yields the source bound a≥ceil(2n+1/2-sqrt(3n²-n+1/4)), asymptotically (2-sqrt3)n. This is a complete known source deduction, not a full proof of one third. 33: Route B: piercing rather than aggregate counts. If three points hit all approval sets, double-counting incidences gives n≤Σ_{j=1}^3 depth(p_j)≤3a. Repeated voters only increase the sum; no distinctness assumption is needed. Choose the component I with smallest right endpoint p, belonging to voter v, whose other component is J. Any component meeting I contains p: it ends no earlier than p and starts no later than p. Consequently every approval set avoiding p must intersect J, since it must intersect I∪J but cannot intersect I. This reduction is exact.

14:                                                    Abstract. Consider a society of voters, each of whom specify an approval
15:                                                    set over a linear political spectrum. We examine double-interval societies, in
16:                                                    which each person’s approval set is represented by two disjoint closed intervals,
17:                                                    and study this situation where the approval sets are pairwise-intersecting:
18:                                                    every pair of voters has a point in the intersection of their approval sets. The
19:                                                    approval ratio for a society is, loosely speaking, the popularity of the most
20:                                                    popular position on the spectrum. We study the question: what is the minimal
21:                                                    guaranteed approval ratio for such a society? We provide a lower bound for the
22:                                                    approval ratio, and examine a family of societies that have rather low approval
23:                                                    ratios. These societies arise from double-n strings: arrangements of n symbols
24:                                                    in which each symbol appears exactly twice.

29:                                                                                 1. Introduction
30:                                                Consider the voting model of Berg et. al.[1] in which a political spectrum X is
31:                                           viewed as a continuum, with liberal positions on the left and conservative positions
32:                                           on the right, and in which each voter v “approves” an interval of positions along
33:                                           this line. For example, a tolerant moderate might approve a wide interval near the
34:                                           middle of the line, while an intolerant partisan may approve a narrower interval
35:                                           near one of the ends.
36:                                                More formally, a society is a spectrum X together with a set of voters V and
37:                                           a collection of approval sets {Av }, one for each voter. A point on the spectrum X
38:                                           is called a platform. In our situation, we imagine X to be R, and each approval set
39:                                           Av is a closed interval that represents the set of all platforms that v approves.
40:                                                Now suppose that every pair of people can agree on some platform; that is, their
41:                                           intervals overlap. In this situation, Helly’s Theorem [3] implies that there exists a
42:                                           point on the line that lies in everyone’s approval set, i.e., there is a platform that
43:                                           everyone approves. Thus a strong hypothesis (pairwise intersecting sets) produces
44:                                           a strong conclusion (a point in all the sets). However, in voting theory, we are
45:                                           usually not looking for unanimity, but may be satisfied with a platform that has
46:                                           high approval ratio: the fraction of voters that approve this platform.
47:                                                Various authors have relaxed the hypotheses. Berg et. al.[1] define a linear
48:                                           (k, m)-agreeable society in which voter preferences again are modeled by closed

76:     We generalize the one-interval model to a society in which every member is
77: identified with two disjoint approval intervals and call such a society a double-
78: interval society. This situation may arise naturally in the context of voting to
79: account for voters who do not place candidates along a linear spectrum in exactly
80: the same order, or to account for voters who find disjoint sets of platforms appealing
81: for entirely different reasons (e.g., for being a party purist, or having the ability
82: to work across party lines). In a scheduling context, such intervals might model a
83: society of workers, each of whom has two different work shifts.
84:     Figure 1 illustrates a double-interval society with four voters. The approval
85: sets of each voter have been separated vertically so they are easier to see. Note
86: that the approval sets are pairwise-intersecting: each voter overlaps every other
87: voter in one or both of their approval intervals. In this example, there are several
88: platforms approved by three voters, but no platform is approved by all four. The
89: approval number of a platform a(p) is the number of voters (in a society S) who
90: approve of platform p. The approval number of a society a(S) is the maximum
91: approval number over all platforms in the spectrum X. That is
92:                                   a(S) = max a(p).
93:                                           p∈X

95: Finally, define the approval ratio of a society to be the approval number of S divided
96: by the number of voters in S.
97:      The main question we address in this paper is: what is the minimal approval
98: ratio of a pairwise-intersecting, double-interval society with n voters?
99:      Examples suggest that the minimal approval ratio of such societies is 1/3; that
100: is, there is always a platform that will get at least a third of the votes. Our results
101: in this paper attempt to clarify this intuition.
102:      We will first examine a family of double-interval societies with low approval ra-
103: tios that have regular patterns of interval overlap. These arise from the construction
104: of what we call double-n strings, defined in the next Section. The combinatorics
105: of such strings are quite nifty and provide a lower bound for the approval ratio of
106: societies in this family (Theorem 3.6) as well as an upper bound (Theorem 3.7) for
107: societies in this family. Roughly speaking, the double-n strings produce societies
108: with asymptotic approval ratios between 0.348 and 0.385.
109:      We will also prove a general lower bound for the approval ratio of any pairwise-
110: intersecting, double-interval society in Theorem 4.1, which shows the approval ratio
111: is always greater than 0.268.

123:                          2. Double-n String Societies
124:     Double-interval societies with regular patterns of interval overlap can be rep-
125: resented by double-n strings, that is, strings of length 2n containing exactly two
126: occurrences of each of n symbols. At times we will also represent double-n strings
127: as strings of the symbols 1, . . . , n. We define the distance between two distinct
128: symbols in a double-n string to be the minimum distance between a pair of occur-
129: rences of the symbols, where the distance between two adjacent symbols is taken
130: as 1. The diameter of a double-n string is the maximum over all 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n of
131: the distance between i and j. We will call two entries in the list adjacent if their
132: positions in the list differ by no more than the diameter of the string.
133:     Let δ(n) be the minimum diameter over all double-n strings.

520:                         6. Conclusion and Open Questions
521:     We have studied pairwise-intersecting double-interval societies, and determined
522: bounds for the minimum guaranteed approval ratio for such societies. Such ques-
523: tions naturally motivated the study of double-n strings, which represent certain
524: special double-interval societies with low approval ratios. Although these do not
525: necessarily provide the smallest such ratios, all of the known examples that provide
526: smaller ratios come from modifying the double-n string construction.
527:     There are numerous open questions.
